About: the Gibbs function of mixing in a two-species lattice model

Source

Concept
Lattice model of a binary mixture: N sites, one molecule on each, a fraction x of species B arranged at random. Per molecule, Δgmix = εx(1 − x) + kBT[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)], with ε > 0 fixed and every energy shown in units of ε.
Serves
Explaining how the shape of Δgmix(x) depends on kBT/ε, both in the middle of the composition range and very close to pure A.
Inquiry
Five questions and a closing summary card. The readouts (in the sidebar panel below the controls) and the logarithmic-axis slope inset appear when a question uses them; all are shown in free exploration.
Misconception
Addressed through the answer choices; each wrong choice has its own feedback, shown only after a choice is made.

Pedagogy principles applied

Commit, then checkEach question is answered before the next card opens and then checked in the sim; the slider and its preset chips are always free to use.
Staged readoutsAt most two numbers are shown while a card is open, and only those that card asks about.
DecompositionThe total curve is drawn with its energy term (red dash-dot) and entropy term (blue dotted) beneath it, so each part can be compared with the total at any temperature.
Stable scaleBoth plots use fixed axes (x from 0 to 1, Δgmix/ε from −0.75 to +0.30; inset x from 10−8 to 0.5, slope from −2 to +1), so every change seen is a change in the physics.
Minima and two phasesBelow kBT = ε/2 open circles mark the two minima of the curve; in free exploration the dashed common tangent joining them shows the composition range in which a mixture splits into two phases.
Instrument viewThe inset's logarithmic composition axis resolves compositions far too small to see on the linear main plot.
Operational numbersThe lowest point in 0 < x ≤ ½ is located numerically from the slope and quoted to three significant figures, in scientific notation below 10−2.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Mixing at kBT = ε

Leave the temperature at kBT = ε. Mixing A and B raises the energy, since ε is positive. The plot shows the energy term and the entropy term; their total appears once you answer. At which compositions does mixing lower the Gibbs function?

2 · Cooling the mixture

Move the temperature slowly down from 1.00 to 0.10 ε/kB, watching the middle of the curve and the curvature readout. What happens to the shape of the curve?

3 · Energy against entropy

Set kBT = 1.00 ε and then 0.30 ε, and compare the red energy curve with the blue entropy curve at x = ½ each time. Why does the hump appear only at low temperature?

4 · A trace of B in pure A

Set kBT = 0.10 ε. On the main plot the curve seems to leave x = 0 rising above zero. Look at the inset and at the lowest-point readout. Does adding a trace of B to pure A lower the Gibbs function?

5 · The minima in the cold

Set kBT = 0.30 ε and read xmin, then lower the temperature to 0.20 ε and 0.10 ε, reading it each time. How does the composition of the left-hand minimum change?

6 · When the two species mix

Above kBT = ε/2 the entropy term wins everywhere: one bowl, and A and B mix in all proportions. Below it the fixed energy term raises a hump between two minima, at xmin and 1 − xmin.

The plot is now at kBT = 0.30 ε. A mixture whose composition lies between the two minima lowers its Gibbs function by splitting into two phases with those compositions, on the dashed common tangent. Outside that range it stays uniform. However cold, xmin ≈ e−ε/kBT is never zero: each species always dissolves a little of the other.

The Physics

Two Species on a Lattice: the Gibbs Function of Mixing · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two species, A and B, share the sites of a lattice, one molecule per site. This sim plots the Gibbs function of mixing per molecule, Δgmix, against the fraction x that are B, and lets you change the temperature kBT/ε.

What you'll learn

  • How Δgmix is built from an energy term and an entropy term.
  • How the shape of the curve depends on kBT/ε, in the middle and close to x = 0.
  • Where the lowest points of the curve sit, and what that says about whether A and B mix.
The lattice model: N sites, one molecule on each, a fraction x of them B, placed at random.

What's on screen

  • Black curve: the total, Δgmix/ε, against x.
  • Red dash-dot curve: the energy term. Blue dotted curve: the entropy term.
  • Slope plot: dΔgmix/dx in units of ε, against x on a logarithmic axis.
  • Readouts: numbers for the middle of the curve and for its left-hand minimum.
See itOpen the sim at its present kBT/ε. Watch for: the three curves on one plot, the slope plot beside it, and the readouts that go with your setting.

Every energy is in units of the fixed ε, which is positive. The plot axes are fixed: Δgmix/ε from −0.75 to +0.30, so a change you see is a change in the physics.

03

Mixing costs energy but gains entropy

Put xN molecules of B and (1 − x)N of A on N sites, at random. An A–B pair costs more energy than the average of an A–A and a B–B pair, by an amount set by ε, and that gives an energy term εx(1 − x) per molecule. Counting the arrangements gives the entropy of mixing, −kB[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)] per molecule, which is positive. The volume does not change, so the pV term drops out, and the second term below is −T times that entropy (notes 6.25).

Notes (6.25).

The energy term does not depend on T, while the entropy term is proportional to T. At kBT = ε and x = ½ they are +0.250 ε and −0.693 ε, so Δgmix(½) = −0.443 ε. The black total is below zero at every composition and lowest at x = ½: at this temperature mixing wins everywhere.

The three curves at kBT = ε, as in the sim. The energy term is the same at every temperature.
See itSet kBT/ε to 1.00. Watch for: the red hump peaking at +0.250, the blue bowl reaching −0.693, and the black total below zero at every x, with Δgmix(½)/ε reading −0.443.
04

Cooling turns the bowl into a hump

The shape comes from the second derivative (notes 6.26, 6.27). The energy term contributes −2ε at every x, whatever the temperature. The entropy term contributes kBT(1/x + 1/(1 − x)), which scales with T.

Notes (6.27), and its value at the middle.

At x = ½ the curvature is −2ε + 4kBT: +2.00 ε at kBT = ε, zero at ε/2, and −1.60 ε at 0.10 ε. Above ε/2 the entropy term wins at every composition: one minimum, at x = ½, and A and B mix in all proportions. Below it the middle rises into a hump, +0.181 ε at 0.10 ε, with a minimum on either side, marked by the open circles.

Δgmix/ε at four temperatures, on the sim's axes. Open circles: the two minima at 0.30.

This is the random-mixing model. The notes call ε/2kB only an estimate of where the hump appears.

See itSet kBT/ε to 0.50. Watch for: the curvature readout at 0.00 and the bottom of the black curve flattened at x = ½.
See itSet kBT/ε to 0.10. Watch for: the curvature reading −1.60, Δgmix(½)/ε reading +0.181, and open circles at the two ends of a curve with a hump in the middle.
05

A trace of B always lowers the Gibbs function

Look at the slope of the curve close to x = 0 (notes 6.26).

Notes (6.26).

As x → 0 the energy part tends to the finite value ε, while kBT ln[x/(1 − x)] tends to −∞. The slope is therefore negative for small enough x, however large ε is, so a little B added to pure A lowers the Gibbs function. The first B molecules gain a lot of entropy, since many sites are open to them, while the energy they bring is only proportional to their number.

At kBT = 0.10 ε the slope is negative below x = 4.54 × 10−5 and Δgmix stays below zero for x < 1.24 × 10−4, at its deepest, −4.54 × 10−6 ε, at that composition. The main plot cannot show a dip that small, which is why the sim adds the slope plot on a logarithmic axis.

The slope at kBT = 0.10 ε, as in the sim's slope plot.
See itSet kBT/ε to 0.10. Watch for: the slope curve in the slope plot starting below zero and crossing zero near 10−4, with the readouts xmin = 4.54 × 10−5 and Δgmin/ε = −4.54 × 10−6.
06

The left-hand minimum falls steeply but never reaches zero

Close to x = 0 the slope is about ε + kBT ln x, which vanishes at xmin ≈ e−ε/kBT. The sim finds xmin numerically; the estimate meets it as the mixture gets colder.

kBT/εxmin, from the sime−ε/kBT
0.300.04630.0357
0.207.19 × 10−36.74 × 10−3
0.104.54 × 10−54.54 × 10−5

From 0.30 ε to 0.10 ε, xmin falls a thousandfold, not threefold as it would in proportion to T, and it reaches zero only at T = 0.

The curve is symmetric, so the other minimum is at 1 − xmin, at the same height. A straight line touching the curve at both is the common tangent (notes 6.35), here horizontal. A mixture whose overall composition lies between the two points can lower its Gibbs function by splitting into those two phases. At 0.30 ε the phases are at 0.0463 and 0.954, where Δgmix = −0.0121 ε, below the +0.042 ε of the uniform mixture at x = ½.

kBT = 0.30 ε. The vertical scale is stretched about tenfold compared with the sim, so the small dip and the hump show. A mixture between the circles can split into those two phases.
See itSet kBT/ε to 0.30. Watch for: open circles at x = 0.0463 and 0.954 joined by the dashed common tangent, and the readouts xmin = 0.0463 and Δgmin/ε = −0.0121.
See itSet kBT/ε to 0.20. Watch for: the circles pushed almost to the two ends, with xmin reading 7.19 × 10−3.
07

Where it matters

  • Solubility. In this model each component of a cold mixture still dissolves a little of the other, an amount that falls steeply, as e−ε/kBT, but is never zero. A pure substance in equilibrium is never quite pure.
  • Phase separation. Two metals or two liquids that cost energy to mix stay uniform when warm and can separate into two phases when cold. The sim's estimate for the onset is kBT = ε/2.
  • Melting points of mixtures. In the notes' binary phase diagram (Figure 47), a little B added to A lowers the temperature at which the solid first appears, for the same reason: B gains entropy by being dispersed in the liquid.
Go deeper: why ε/2 is only an estimate

Counting the arrangements and the energy both assume the species sit at random, which holds while |ε| is small compared with kBT. At kBT = ε/2, ε is twice kBT, so real species cluster somewhat instead. The notes therefore read ε/2kB as an estimate of where separation sets in, and the sim says so beside the temperature control.

08

Summary

In one line. The sim plots the Gibbs function of mixing of two species on a lattice, split into an energy term and an entropy term, against the composition x at a temperature you choose.

Key points

  • Δgmix is a fixed energy cost plus an entropy gain proportional to T.
  • Above kBT = ε/2 the curve is one bowl; below it, a hump between two minima.
  • Near x = 0 the slope is always negative, so a trace of B always dissolves; xmin ≈ e−ε/kBT.

Common mix-ups

  • “Mixing raises the energy, so the species stay apart.” At kBT = ε the entropy term, −0.693 ε at x = ½, outweighs the energy term, +0.250 ε.
  • “The energy term grows as the temperature falls.” It is εx(1 − x) at every setting; the entropy term shrinks, from −0.693 ε to −0.208 ε at x = ½ between 1.00 and 0.30.
  • “At 0.10 ε the curve rises from x = 0, so nothing dissolves.” The slope is negative below x = 4.54 × 10−5; the dip is just too small to see.

Things to try on your own

  • Slide kBT/ε down from 1.00 and note where the curvature readout changes sign.
  • Predict Δgmix(½) at 0.40 ε from the two terms, then set it, and say whether the middle is a minimum or a maximum.
  • Read xmin at 0.30, 0.20 and 0.10 and compare each with e−ε/kBT.
